title: Saif Ali Khan Learns to Make Puris With Soldiers in Uri for Independence Day
excerpt: The actor joined NDTV's Jai Jawan programme to mark India's 80th Independence Day, spending time with jawans at an army cookhouse in Jammu and Kashmir.
body:
• Actor Saif Ali Khan visited an army post in Uri, Jammu and Kashmir, for NDTV's Jai Jawan programme on India's 80th Independence Day.
  • Khan learned to make puris for the first time in the army cookhouse, taking lessons from a jawan before serving the soldiers lunch.
  • The visit also included playing guitar and cricket with soldiers, and a trip to the Kaman Aman Setu bridge on the Jhelum River.

On India's 80th Independence Day, Bollywood actor Saif Ali Khan traded a film set for an army cookhouse in Uri, rolling up his sleeves to learn what generations of Indian soldiers have mastered in the field: the art of making a proper puri.

Khan was in Jammu and Kashmir for NDTV's Jai Jawan, the network's long-running programme that pairs celebrities with Indian Armed Forces personnel in remote postings. Accompanied by anchor Meenakshi Kandwal, the actor travelled to a forward post in Uri — a town whose name carries deep significance in India's military history, most recently as the site of the 2016 terror attack that prompted cross-border surgical strikes.

First Puris, Imperfect Circles

In the compact army cookhouse, equipped with everything needed to feed an entire unit, Khan observed the efficient setup with characteristic understatement. "Actually, you just need a small fire to cook food," he remarked.

Speaking modestly about his own kitchen credentials, the actor added: "While I am no super chef, I do spend a lot of time in the kitchen."

His puri-making debut, however, told a different story. Taking instruction from a jawan, Khan attempted to shape the dough — and produced what he readily acknowledged were uneven forms rather than the perfectly round discs that army cooks turn out by the hundred. The moment drew laughter from the soldiers watching.

The puris were fried nonetheless, and Khan served them to the jawans before sitting down together for lunch — a meal of dal, rice, puri and sabzi with a side salad. It was army cooking at its most elemental: simple ingredients, shared among people doing difficult work in a difficult place.

Cricket, Guitar and a Bridge Built in Six Hours

Food was only part of the visit. Khan, a well-known cricket enthusiast, joined the soldiers for a match. "Cricket is another bonding sport. When you play with people, it makes you respect them on a different level," he said. "I had a lot of fun."

He also entertained the troops by playing guitar — a reminder that the Pataudi scion's off-screen interests extend well beyond film.

Khan visited the Kaman Aman Setu on the Jhelum River, a bridge the Indian Army constructed in just six hours. Dressed in a bulletproof jacket and travelling in an armoured Casper vehicle, the actor trekked through the terrain and tried his hand at the gun range, describing the experience as "tiring" but exciting.

A Tradition That Resonates

NDTV's Jai Jawan has become one of India's most recognisable Independence Day traditions, sending actors and public figures to spend time with soldiers at remote postings. Previous editions have featured stars including Aamir Khan in Kargil, John Abraham with the army in 2024, and Bhumi Pednekar for Republic Day 2026.

For diaspora Indians watching from abroad, the programme offers a rare and intimate glimpse of everyday life at India's forward posts — where the routines are demanding, the terrain unforgiving, and a shared meal of puris and dal carries a significance that goes well beyond the plate.
image_caption: Saif Ali Khan visited the army forward post at Uri for NDTV Jai Jawan 2026, where soldiers taught him to make puris in the field cookhouse on Independence Day.
nri_angle: The Jai Jawan programme, which pairs Bollywood stars with Indian soldiers in remote postings, has become an Independence Day tradition that resonates deeply with the diaspora. For NRIs watching from abroad, it offers a window into the everyday lives of soldiers serving in some of India's most challenging terrain — and a reminder that a shared meal of dal, puri and sabzi remains one of the most universal expressions of Indian community.
